author: Codex Designer rehearsal, 2026-11-10. Interpretations, proposed root and guesses are agent-authored.
stage_status: Stages 0 and 1 rehearsal only. No completion, sent asks, owner approval, waiver, stage result, item filing or ledger write.

root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: Warscar makes scavenging an old battlefield feel cursed for reasons the player can see and act on. Its poisoned ground supports creatures that live on the war's remains; apparently placid armour can turn murderous, a breathing stretch of wall can stand up, and a hunter can be known by the traces around its invisible body. When the wind stills, toxic dust falls and records movement; returning wind lifts that record away. Broken guns follow passers-by without firing. The same ruins offer powerful prizes: working projectors to carry home, chemistry to harvest, manuals that unlock practical improvements, and deserted machines whose names and histories survive repair or failure. Staying leaves a lasting mark that teaches useful work as it burdens the survivor. Protection and knowledge make expeditions more capable, and the technology remains broadly useful beyond this biome. The free biome holds that experience on its own; campaign discoveries and ship-vermin behaviour belong to their existing neighbours. Each built promise needs a demonstration, including where the promises meet.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: ASK FIRST — The promise behind the curse
asks.picture: The crew brings home a working projector and an intact machine. One scavenger carries a lasting mark. They understand the risks better than on arrival, and already have a reason to go back.
asks.text: What should make you think “they learned why it is cursed” in that return-home moment, and which part of my root gets that wrong?
asks.decision: If the personal cost leads, the return-home scene must show the lasting mark alongside the prize. If discovery leads, the scene must connect what was found to the battlefield without revealing campaign secrets. If temptation leads, it must show a concrete next expedition worth its price. These are emphasis and acceptance choices; all built systems retain coverage. A correction rewrites the root before dependent claims are bound.
asks.why: F1/F3. “Cursed” could rest on an enduring personal cost, unsettling discoveries, or the way practical gains tempt another visit. The chosen sentence does not rank those consequences.
asks.guess: The temptation matters because the costs are real and remembered. I would lead with a successful expedition that changes somebody.

If discovery leads, the scene must connect what was found to the battlefield without revealing campaign secrets. If temptation leads, it must show a concrete next expedition worth its price. asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: ASK FIRST — The first demonstration
asks.picture: A, a salvage party takes shelter under a humming ring during a Settling, reads the tracks outside and decides when to carry the ring away. B, a deserter passes through diagnosis, lights, limbs, voice and waking, with a separately demonstrated named failure. C, ordinary work beside apparently quiet wildlife turns into a response to a chatrak or a waking wall.
asks.text: Which of those would you put first to judge whether Warscar understands you, and what single failure there would make you stop the demonstration?
asks.decision: A makes shelter and extraction the first showcase; B makes recovery and identity first; C makes the deceptive battlefield first. Each answer also supplies a rejection case. The other capabilities still need their own scenes, and interactions need explicit checks. Only a real flagship pick can bind showcase 1; root approval alone cannot.
asks.why: F1/F2/F3. I found no recorded choice of this mod's flagship under the current showcase contract.
asks.guess: A joins the poisoned ground, useful technology and salvage decision most directly. I recommend it first, then a separate hospice demonstration.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: The invisible hunter while you are watching somewhere else
asks.picture: A lone night hauler passes through glower. A moving patch of ticking falls silent; when there is film, prints cross it with no animal above them. The camera is at the workshop. A second colonist is close enough to make the hauler company.
asks.text: Which of those signs should reach you in time to change the hauler's orders, and which may be a discovery you make afterwards?
asks.decision: If local observation is enough, judge an actual approach at play zoom and with sound, plus the existing company protection. If a remote warning is essential, add a narrowly triggered warning and a control with no approaching hunter. If signs may explain the aftermath, require a trace that remains interpretable after the attack; do not silently claim advance warning. Group safety remains an existing obligation in every branch.
asks.why: F2. Prints, silence, shimmer and strike reveal are already built or specified. Their existence alone does not settle whether an off-camera ambush was fairly readable.
asks.guess: On camera, movement and silence should give an attentive player a chance; ordinary off-camera travel should remain manageable through company rather than a new warning for every hunter.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: What the chatrak's warning buys
asks.picture: A scaria chatrak near the work area lifts its plates, stops feeding and begins circling. Workers are dispersed; one animal is tethered nearby. The stages and eventual rage are already part of the build.
asks.text: By the circling stage, what should a careful player still have time to get out of its way?
asks.decision: A local retreat requires an observed warning-to-danger interval with ordinary movement and a blocked-route reject case. A whole-worksite evacuation needs a dispersed-party scene and enough earlier notice. If circling is already the point of no safe response, bind the earlier plate change as the actionable warning and judge circling as imminent danger. None of these branches reopens scaria onset or the settled clean-animal distinction.
asks.why: F2. Setting a stage directly proves its state, but says nothing about the useful time between noticing it and the snap.
asks.guess: Nearby people and a sensibly managed animal should have a fair retreat; a whole settlement should not be rebuilt during that last warning.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: Repair when the safer part is late
asks.picture: A named deserter has reached the limbs stage. Etchant is available, but the haulers are busy. The current cradle waits six in-game hours, then starts a slower and riskier repair without it. Its memories and eventual usefulness are already part of the promise.
asks.text: What should tell the cradle to take that extra risk when the safer part is merely late: your order, a standing repair policy, or elapsed time?
asks.decision: A direct order needs a waiting state and an explicit proceed-without-etchant action. A standing policy needs saved per-cradle behaviour and a test with delayed hauling. Elapsed time needs the deadline and extra risk stated before it expires, plus a clear account of the failure if it occurs. Every branch preserves the etchant-free repair route, the named failure wreck, the accepted histories and the strong worker.
asks.why: F1/F3. Repair without etchant is already allowed. The unresolved choice is who commits a particular machine to that risk when a routine hauling delay looks the same as a shortage.
asks.guess: A standing repair policy, visible on the cradle, with an explicit choice for this machine. I would default to waiting when etchant exists and is reachable.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: Taking the shelter home
asks.picture: The only working ring shelters the party's supplies and an injured scavenger. Its condition has been evaluated. A colonist finishes uninstalling it, and the clean circle disappears while the Settling continues. Losing the dome when the ring is taken is already the intended trade.
asks.text: Before that last action completes, what should make the exposed people and supplies clear to you: the order's explanation, a warning when work begins, or the changing scene itself?
asks.decision: An order explanation needs a truthful command description and a consequence check. A conditional warning needs a defined dependency test and a control where another screen still protects the occupants. Scene-only communication needs a witnessed transition that makes the exposed area clear without reading an alert. Working-ring salvage stays available in every case.
asks.why: F1/F2. A salvage job can be mechanically correct while hiding the consequence from the person who ordered it.
asks.guess: The order should state the loss of shelter clearly; an extra interruption earns its place only when somebody is actually relying on that dome.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: The beautiful phase that burns
asks.picture: Before the phase reader is unlocked, a tap shows an unknown colour and a phase icon. The colony has ordered repeated draws. During the walk to the tap the pool changes to bloom; drawing it produces valuable liquor and burns the worker's hand.
asks.text: What should let you distinguish a deliberate dangerous harvest from an ordinary job that unexpectedly burns its worker?
asks.decision: If the order carries the warning, require an explicit risk description and a phase-change-during-walk case. If the changing phase must communicate the risk, judge a labelled exploration of that transition before prescribing a cue. If the first injury teaches the consequence, bind the lasting journal and cause-of-injury explanation, and do not claim the first draw was warned safe. Existing bloom harvesting and the researched skip control remain in all branches.
asks.why: F1/F2. The bloom's injury, journal and later skip control are already specified. The missing acceptance choice is what the order commits the player to before that safety knowledge exists.
asks.guess: The standing order should plainly include the dangerous phase, with a readable last chance to stop it. The phase reader can still provide the better automatic control later.

asks.speaker: agent
asks.title: A settlement large enough to miss things
asks.picture: Forty colonists have an established workday here. The wind stills while one cradle waits for a part, a tap is drawing, and crews are sweeping dust and salvaging. The mark, risks and useful jobs continue; the player has other colony problems too.
asks.text: Which change should interrupt that workday, and which should the colony handle through standing orders while you watch elsewhere?
asks.decision: If new exposure is the interruption, add a shared-condition scene with protected and exposed crews. If each major event demands attention, judge the actual combined message sequence and its deduplication. If standing orders should cover known hazards, specify which order is relied on and show it working while another task occupies the player. This selects communication and routine-work bars, not permission to suppress any built capability.
asks.why: F1/F3. “Atmosphere” can become constant alert dismissal, and “danger” can become unnoticed harm. The source sets mechanics and some messages, but does not establish an attention budget for mature play.
asks.guess: A newly unsafe work area deserves attention; routine known production and waiting for a part should remain ordinary work, with details available on inspection.
